l: golden goblet, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: The Sun gives Hercules a golden goblet after admiring his courage. Hercules uses it to cross the ocean to Erythia and later returns it to the Sun at Tartessus.

l: Cretan Bull, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: A bull escapes from Hercules' herd at Rhegium, plunges into the sea, and swims across to Sicily. It reaches the plain of Eryx, where Eryx mingles it with his own herds.

l: Eryx, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Eryx is a son of Poseidon and king of the Elymi. He refuses to surrender the escaped bull unless Hercules defeats him in wrestling; Hercules defeats him three times and kills him.

l: Hera, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hera sends a gadfly that causes the kine to scatter among the foothills of Thrace. Eurystheus later sacrifices the recovered kine to her.

l: The Library, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: After Hercules had completed his labours in eight years and a month, Eurystheus assigned him an eleventh labour: fetching golden apples from the Hesperides. The apples were said to be located by Atlas in Hyperborea rather than in Libya, and to have been given by Earth to Zeus when he married Hera. An immortal, hundred-headed dragon born of Typhon and Echidna guarded the apples, together with the Hesperides. On his journey, Hercules reached the river Echedorus, where Cycnus challenged him to single combat, but a thunderbolt separated them.

l: Hercules, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: After completing his labours in eight years and a month, Hercules was ordered to undertake an eleventh labour: fetching the golden apples from the Hesperides. While traveling to the apples, he reached the river Echedorus, where Cycnus challenged him to single combat.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: After Hercules had completed his labours in eight years and a month, Eurystheus ordered him to fetch the golden apples as an eleventh labour.

l: the labours of Hercules, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: The labours of Hercules had been performed in eight years and a month before Eurystheus assigned the eleventh labour.

l: the eleventh labour, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: The eleventh labour was the task of fetching golden apples from the Hesperides.

l: golden apples, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: The golden apples were said to be located by Atlas in Hyperborea, not in Libya as some claimed. Earth gave them to Zeus when he married Hera, and they were guarded by an immortal dragon and the Hesperides.

l: Hesperides, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: The Hesperides guarded the golden apples together with the immortal dragon.

l: Zeus, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: Zeus received the golden apples from Earth when he married Hera.

l: Hera, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: Hera was married by Zeus when Earth gave the golden apples to him.

l: dragon of the Hesperides, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: The dragon of the Hesperides was an immortal offspring of Typhon and Echidna. It had one hundred heads and used many different and varied voices to guard the golden apples.

l: Apollodorus, The Library, When the labours had been performed in eight
s: Apollodorus records that Eurystheus assigned Hercules the eleventh labour of fetching the golden apples and describes their location and guardians.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Hercules travels through Illyria, Libya, Egypt, Asia, Arabia, and beyond in pursuit of the golden apples. He defeats Antaeus, kills Busiris and his son, rescues Prometheus, and obtains the apples through a trick involving Atlas. Hercules gives the apples to Eurystheus, though another tradition says he plucked them himself after killing the guardian snake.

l: Hesperides, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: The Hesperides guard the golden apples together with an immortal dragon. They are named Aegle, Erythia, Hesperia, and Arethusa.

l: golden apples, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: The golden apples were presented by Earth to Zeus after his marriage with Hera and were guarded by the Hesperides and an immortal dragon. Atlas brings three of them to Hercules, who gives them to Eurystheus; another account says Hercules plucks them himself after killing the guardian snake.

l: Libya, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Hercules traverses Libya while seeking the golden apples. At that time, Libya is ruled by Antaeus.

l: Atlas, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Atlas is relieved by Hercules of the burden of the sphere while he obtains three golden apples from the Hesperides. Hercules tricks Atlas into taking the sphere back by asking him to hold it while Hercules puts a pad on his head.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: The golden apples are presented to Zeus by Earth after his marriage with Hera. Busiris sacrifices strangers on an altar of Zeus according to an oracle.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Hercules learns from Nereus where the golden apples and the Hesperides are, defeats Antaeus, kills Busiris and his son, and rescues Prometheus. He obtains the apples through Atlas and gives them to Eurystheus.

l: Antaeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Antaeus, son of Poseidon, rules Libya and kills strangers by forcing them to wrestle. Hercules lifts him from the earth, breaks him, and kills him because he becomes stronger when touching the ground.

l: Egypt, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Hercules traverses Egypt after passing through Libya. Egypt is then ruled by Busiris.

l: Busiris, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Busiris sacrifices strangers to Zeus because an oracle says this will end Egypt's nine-year dearth. He captures Hercules for sacrifice, but Hercules breaks his bonds and kills Busiris and his son Amphidamas.

l: Prometheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Prometheus is chained on the Caucasus while an eagle, offspring of Echidna and Typhon, eats his liver. Hercules shoots the eagle, releases Prometheus, and provides Chiron as a willing immortal substitute who will die in his place.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. v. 11
s: Eurystheus receives the golden apples from Hercules.

l: The Library, The Library, 12
s: The twelfth labor required Hercules to bring Cerberus from Hades. Cerberus had three dog heads, a serpent’s tail, and many snake heads along his back. Before going to him, Hercules went to Eumolpus at Eleusis to be initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, but first had to be purified because he had not been cleansed from the killing of the Centaurs. After Eumolpus purified him, he was initiated, and he later came to Tainaron in Laconia.

l: Hercules, The Library, 12
s: Hercules was assigned the twelfth labor of bringing Cerberus from Hades. Before undertaking it, he went to Eumolpus at Eleusis for initiation into the Eleusinian Mysteries and was purified from the killing of the Centaurs.

l: Cerberus, The Library, 12
s: Cerberus was the subject of Hercules’ twelfth labor. He had three dog heads, a serpent’s tail, and many snake heads along his back.

l: Hades, The Library, 12
s: Hades was the place from which Hercules was ordered to bring Cerberus.

l: Eumolpus, The Library, 12
s: Eumolpus received Hercules at Eleusis and purified him from the killing of the Centaurs. Afterward, Hercules was initiated.

l: Eleusis, The Library, 12
s: Eleusis was where Hercules went to Eumolpus because he wished to be initiated.

l: Eleusinian initiation, The Library, 12
s: The Eleusinian Mysteries were not then open to foreigners. Hercules could not initially see them because he had not been purified from the killing of the Centaurs, but after Eumolpus purified him, he was initiated.

l: Tainaron, The Library, 12
s: Tainaron in Laconia was the place to which Hercules came after his initiation.

l: twelfth labor of Hercules, The Library, 12
s: The twelfth labor of Hercules was to bring Cerberus from Hades.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Hercules descends into Hades through Taenarum to fetch Cerberus, encounters Theseus and Pirithous, and brings Cerberus to Eurystheus before returning him to Hades. After his labours, Hercules gives Megara to Iolaus, seeks to marry Iole, and kills Iphitus after a fit of madness. To be cured, he is sold by Hermes to Omphale for three years as compensation for the murder. During his servitude, Hercules performs various deeds, including seizing the Cercopes, killing Syleus, burying Icarus, and participating in the voyage to Colchis and the Calydonian hunt.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Hercules descends into Hades through Taenarum to fetch Cerberus. He raises Theseus but cannot bring up Pirithous, wrestles Menoetes, obtains Cerberus from Pluto without using his weapons, brings the beast to Eurystheus, and returns it to Hades. Afterward, he gives Megara to Iolaus, fails to obtain Iole from Eurytus, kills Iphitus in a fit of madness, and is sold to Omphale for three years to remedy his disease and pay compensation for the murder. During his servitude, he seizes the Cercopes, kills Syleus and Xenodice, buries Icarus, and is said to take part in the voyage to Colchis and the Calydonian hunt.

l: Cerberus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Cerberus has three dog heads, a dragon’s tail, and snake heads on his back. Pluto permits Hercules to take him if Hercules masters him without his weapons. Hercules finds him at the gates of Acheron, grips and chokes him despite being bitten by the dragon in his tail, carries him to Eurystheus, and then returns him to Hades.

l: Hades, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Hercules descends into Hades through the entrance at Taenarum. The souls flee from him except Meleager and Medusa, and near the gates he finds Theseus and Pirithous bound. Hercules later returns Cerberus to Hades after displaying him to Eurystheus.

l: Theseus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Theseus is found by Hercules near the gates of Hades, where he is bound because he joined Pirithous in wooing Persephone. He stretches out his hands toward Hercules, and Hercules takes him by the hand and raises him.

l: Eurytus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Eurytus, prince of Oechalia, offers his daughter Iole as a prize to whoever can defeat him and his sons in archery. Although Hercules proves superior in archery, Eurytus refuses to give him Iole because he fears Hercules may again kill his children. Eurytus suspects Hercules of stealing cattle from Euboea, and later refuses to accept compensation for Iphitus’s murder.

l: Omphale, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIT. v. r1-12
s: Omphale, daughter of Iardanes and queen of Lydia, buys Hercules from Hermes after an oracle orders that he be sold and serve for three years. Hercules serves Omphale as a slave and performs several deeds during that servitude.

l: The Library, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: After recovering from his illness following the sacrifice, Heracles sailed to Ilium with eighteen penteconters and an army of willing distinguished men. He left the ships under Oicles and advanced on the city with the other nobles, but Laomedon killed Oicles while fighting. Heracles's forces besieged Laomedon, and Telamon broke through the wall and entered first, followed by Heracles. Heracles captured the city, shot Laomedon and his sons except Podarces, and awarded Hesione, Laomedon's daughter, to Telamon.

l: Hercules, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Heracles sailed to Ilium with eighteen penteconters and an army of distinguished men who willingly wanted to campaign. He besieged Laomedon, entered the city after Telamon, captured the city, shot Laomedon and his sons except Podarces, and awarded Hesione to Telamon.

l: Telamon, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: During the siege, Telamon broke through the wall and entered Ilium first, before Heracles. Heracles awarded Hesione to Telamon after the capture of the city.

l: Laomedon, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Laomedon came against the ships with the multitude and killed Oicles while fighting. After being driven back by Heracles's men, he was besieged; when the city was captured, Heracles shot him.

l: Hesione, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Hesione is identified as Laomedon's daughter. After Heracles captured the city, he awarded her to Telamon.

l: Troy, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Heracles sailed to Ilium and attacked it with an army. Ilium was besieged and captured after Telamon broke through its wall.

l: the city of Troy, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Heracles's forces besieged the city after Laomedon was driven back. Telamon entered first through a breach in the wall, Heracles followed, and Heracles then captured the city.

l: voyage to Troy, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: After recovering from his illness following the sacrifice, Heracles sailed to Ilium with eighteen penteconters. He brought an army of distinguished men who willingly wanted to campaign.

l: siege of Troy, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: After Laomedon killed Oicles and was driven back by Heracles's men, Laomedon was besieged. During the siege, Telamon broke through the wall and entered first, followed by Heracles.

l: capture of Troy, The Library, Μετὰ δὲ τὴν λατρείαν ἀπαλλαγεὶς τῆς νόσου
s: Heracles captured Ilium after entering it behind Telamon. He shot Laomedon and his sons except Podarces and awarded Hesione to Telamon.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Hercules captures Troy, Cos, Elis, and Pylus, defeats several enemies, and establishes or celebrates religious rites at Olympia. He later attacks Lacedaemon to avenge the death of Licymnius’s son, restores Tyndareus to power, and encounters Auge and her infant son Telephus. At Calydon, Hercules wins Deianira as his wife after defeating Achelous and receives the horn of Amaltheia in exchange for Achelous’s broken horn.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Hercules captures Troy, takes Cos by night, joins the gods against the Giants at Phlegra, conquers Elis and Pylus, and defeats Hippocoon and his sons. He kills Augeas, restores Phyleus to the throne, establishes Olympic rites, and later restores Tyndareus to the kingdom of Lacedaemon. He unknowingly fathers Telephus with Auge and marries Deianira after defeating Achelous.

l: Troy, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Troy is besieged and captured by Hercules after Telamon breaches its wall first. Laomedon and his sons, except Podarces, are killed, and Hesione is awarded to Telamon.

l: Augeas, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Augeas appoints Eurytus and Cteatus as generals against Hercules. Hercules later captures Elis, kills Augeas and his sons, and gives the kingdom to Phyleus.

l: Elis, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Elis sends the Molionides to participate in the sacrifices at the third Isthmian festival. Hercules ambushes and kills them at Cleonae, then marches against Elis and captures the city.

l: Auge, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Auge, daughter of Aleus, is unknowingly violated by Hercules and secretly gives birth to a child. Aleus discovers her pregnancy, and Auge is given to Nauplius, who takes her to Teuthras in Mysia; Teuthras makes her his wife.

l: Telephus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Telephus is born to Auge and Hercules and is exposed on Mount Parthenius. A doe provides milk for him, shepherds rescue him, and they name him Telephus.

l: Deianira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vr. 3-4
s: Deianira, daughter of Oeneus, is sought in marriage by Hercules at Calydon. Hercules wins her by defeating Achelous, who had taken the form of a bull.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Hercules came to Calydon and married Deianira after wrestling Achelous, who had taken the form of a bull. Hercules broke off one of Achelous’s horns, and Achelous recovered it by receiving Amalthea’s horn, which could provide abundant meat or drink. Hercules later campaigned with the Calydonians against Thesprotous, captured a city, and fathered Tlepolemus by Astyoche.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Hercules came to Calydon and wooed Deianira, defeating Achelous in the struggle for her hand by breaking off one of his horns. He later campaigned with the Calydonians against Thesprotous, captured a city ruled by Phylas, and fathered Tlepolemus by Astyoche. While staying among the Thesprotous, he sent sons to Thebes and Sardinia for colonization.

l: Calydon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Calydon was the place where Hercules wooed and married Deianira. Its people later campaigned with Hercules against Thesprotous.

l: Deianira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Deianira was the daughter of Oeneus. Hercules won her in marriage after wrestling with Achelous.

l: Achelous, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Achelous assumed the likeness of a bull while competing with Hercules for Deianira. Hercules broke off one of his horns, and Achelous recovered it by giving Amalthea’s horn in exchange.

l: Amalthea's horn, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Amalthea’s horn was given by Achelous in exchange for the horn Hercules had broken off. According to Pherecydes, it could supply whatever meat or drink was desired in abundance.

l: Thesprotous, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vis. 4-5
s: Hercules campaigned against Thesprotous with the Calydonians and captured a city ruled by Phylas. He remained among the Thesprotous and sent sons to Thebes and Sardinia for colonization.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Hercules marched with the Calydonians against the Thesprotians, took Ephyra, and fathered Tlepolemus with Astyoche. While feasting with Oeneus, he accidentally killed Eunomus, then accepted exile and set out toward Trachis with Deianeira. At the river Evenus, Nessus attempted to assault Deianeira while ferrying her, so Heracles shot him in the heart. Dying, Nessus gave Deianeira instructions for making a love charm from his blood and the substance from his wound.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Hercules marched with the Calydonians against the Thesprotians and took the city of Ephyra. After accidentally killing Eunomus while feasting with Oeneus, he chose to undergo exile and set out toward Trachis with Deianeira.

l: Oeneus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Oeneus was feasting with Hercules when Eunomus, his kinsman, was accidentally killed.

l: Eunomus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Eunomus, the son of Architeles and a kinsman of Oeneus, was pouring water on Hercules's hands when Hercules struck and killed him with his knuckles.

l: Eunomus's accidental killing, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Hercules accidentally killed Eunomus while Eunomus was pouring water on his hands during a feast with Oeneus. Because the killing was an accident, it was treated as a matter for which Hercules would undergo exile.

l: Deianira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Deianeira traveled with Hercules toward Trachis. At the river Evenus, Nessus attempted to assault her while ferrying her; afterward, Nessus told her how to prepare a love charm for Hercules from material connected with his wound, and she kept it.

l: Evenus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Evenus was the river Hercules and Deianeira reached while traveling toward Trachis. Hercules crossed it himself, while Nessus ferried Deianeira.

l: Nessus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Nessus the Centaur ferried passersby across the river Evenus for payment, claiming that the gods had granted him this service because of his justice. While carrying Deianeira, he attempted to assault her, and as he was dying he gave her instructions for preparing a love charm for Hercules.

l: Nessus's attempted assault on Deianeira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: Nessus attempted to assault Deianeira while ferrying her across Evenus. Deianeira cried out, and Hercules became aware of what was happening.

l: Heracles's shooting of Nessus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 6
s: After hearing Deianeira cry out during Nessus's attempted assault, Heracles shot Nessus in the heart with an arrow. As Nessus was about to die, he spoke to Deianeira about making a love charm for Hercules from his blood and material from his wound.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Hercules travels with Deianira to Trachis, defeats the Dryopes and other opponents, and later captures Oechalia from Eurytus, taking Iole captive. Deianira, fearing that Hercules will love Iole more than her, treats a tunic with what she believes is a love charm made from Nessus's blood. The Hydra's poison in the tunic corrodes Hercules's body, leading Deianira to commit suicide and Hercules to order a pyre built on Mount Oeta. Hercules dies on the pyre and is taken to heaven, where he becomes immortal and reconciles with Hera.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Hercules travels to Trachis with Deianira, defeats the Dryopes, aids Aegimius against the Lapiths, kills Cycnus and Amyntor, and captures Oechalia from Eurytus. After Deianira treats his tunic with Nessus's blood, the Hydra's poison corrodes his body; he is carried to Trachis, orders a pyre built on Mount Oeta, and becomes immortal after his death.

l: Trachis, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Trachis is the destination to which Hercules travels with Deianira, where Ceyx receives him. Hercules later returns to Trachis after being afflicted by the poisoned tunic.

l: Deianira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Deianira travels with Hercules and keeps the substance Nessus gives her as a supposed love charm. Fearing that Hercules will prefer Iole, she applies it to his tunic; after seeing what happens to him, she hangs herself.

l: Nessus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Nessus ferries Deianira across the river Evenus and attempts to violate her. Hercules shoots him through the heart, and while dying Nessus deceives Deianira by presenting his blood as a love charm.

l: love charm for Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: The supposed love charm consists of material associated with Nessus's blood and the seed he dropped on the ground. Deianira believes it will make Hercules love her, but it instead causes the destruction of his body when applied to his tunic.

l: Nessus's blood, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Nessus tells Deianira to mix his blood with the seed he dropped and preserve it as a love charm. Deianira later smears it on Hercules's tunic, where it carries the Hydra's poison.

l: Oechalia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Oechalia is attacked and captured by Hercules after he gathers an army to punish Eurytus. Its city is pillaged, and Iole is taken captive.

l: Eurytus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Eurytus is the ruler of Oechalia. Hercules attacks him, kills him and his sons, and takes Oechalia.

l: Iole, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Iole is captured by Hercules when he takes Oechalia. Hercules later charges Hyllus to marry her when Hyllus has grown to manhood.

l: tunic, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Deianira smears the tunic with what she believes is a love charm before Hercules wears it for a sacrifice. When it is warmed, the Hydra's poison causes it to cling to Hercules's body and tear away his flesh when he removes it.

l: Hydra's poison, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: The Hydra's poison is present in the material from Nessus's wound. When the treated tunic is warmed, the poison corrodes Hercules's skin and brings about his death.

l: Mount Oeta, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Mount Oeta is where Hercules goes after being afflicted by the tunic. He orders a pyre to be made there.

l: pyre, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Hercules orders a pyre to be made on Mount Oeta and asks someone to set it alight. No one initially agrees, but Poeas lights it while passing by in search of his flocks.

l: death of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Hercules's death follows the corrosion of his body by the Hydra's poison in the tunic. He is taken to the pyre on Mount Oeta, which is set alight, and a cloud with thunder carries him to heaven.

l: apotheosis of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: After the pyre burns, Hercules is carried to heaven in a cloud accompanied by thunder. He receives immortality and is reconciled with Hera.

l: capture of Oechalia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Hercules captures Oechalia with the aid of Arcadians, Melians from Trachis, and Epicnemidian Locrians. He kills Eurytus and his sons, takes the city, pillages it, and leads Iole away captive.

l: suicide of Deianira, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vu. 6-7
s: Deianira learns what has happened to Hercules after he wears the treated tunic. She hangs herself.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Hercules went to Oeta in the Trachinian territory, built a pyre, and was carried to heaven when a cloud and thunder lifted him from the burning pyre. He became immortal, married Hebe, and had sons, including Alexiares and Anicetus, as well as many sons by the daughters of Thespius and other women. After Hercules was translated to the gods, his sons, also called the Heraclids, fled from Eurystheus to Athens, where the Athenians protected them and fought Eurystheus. The Athenians killed Eurystheus's sons, and Hyllus pursued and killed Eurystheus, giving his head to Alcmena.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Hercules went to Oeta in the Trachinian territory and constructed a pyre. While the pyre burned, a cloud carried him to heaven with a peal of thunder, after which he obtained immortality, married Hebe, and had numerous sons by Hebe, the daughters of Thespius, and other women.

l: Mount Oeta, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Oeta was the place in the Trachinian territory where Hercules constructed his pyre and was carried up to heaven.

l: pyre, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Hercules constructed the pyre on Oeta and ordered it to be kindled. When no one else would light it, Poeas set it alight while Hercules mounted it.

l: Hyllus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Hyllus pursued Eurystheus as he fled in a chariot near the Scironian cliffs and killed him.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Eurystheus demanded that the sons of Hercules be surrendered and threatened war when they were sheltered by Ceyx. After his sons were killed by the Athenians, Eurystheus fled in a chariot, but Hyllus pursued and killed him; his head was given to Alcmena.

l: sons of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: After Hercules was translated to the gods, his sons fled from Eurystheus and sought refuge first with Ceyx and then in Athens. The Athenians protected them, and they later came to the Peloponnese and seized all its cities after Eurystheus was killed.

l: Trachis, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Trachis was the place the sons of Hercules left when they fled from Eurystheus through Greece.

l: Athens, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Athens received the pursued sons of Hercules, who sat at the altar of Mercy and requested protection. The Athenians defended them there against Eurystheus.

l: Athenians, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: The Athenians refused to surrender the sons of Hercules to Eurystheus and undertook war against him. They killed Eurystheus's sons, Alexander, Iphimedon, Eurybius, Mentor, and Perimedes.

l: war with Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: The Athenians undertook the war with Eurystheus because they refused to surrender the sons of Hercules. During the conflict, the Athenians killed Eurystheus's sons.

l: Alcmena, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: Hyllus gave Alcmena the severed head of Eurystheus. Alcmena gouged out Eurystheus's eyes with weaving-pins.

l: Heraclids, The Library, THE LIBRARY, IIL. vir. 7
s: The sons of Hercules are identified as the Heraclids after Hercules was translated to the gods. They fled from Eurystheus, sought protection in Athens, and later went to the Peloponnese and seized all its cities.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The Heraclids repeatedly attempt to return to the Peloponnese, interpreting an oracle about the third crop and the narrows before finally conquering the region under Oxylus's guidance. Aristodemus dies at Naupactus, and his sons Eurysthenes and Procles later share Lacedaemon after the drawing of lots, while Temenus receives Argos and Cresphontes receives Messene. The rulers establish signs for their territories, but Temenus's sons murder him because he favors Hyrnetho and Deiphontes. Cresphontes and two of his sons are murdered by Polyphontes, but his surviving son Aepytus returns secretly, kills Polyphontes, and recovers the kingdom.

l: Heraclids, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The Heraclids leave the Peloponnese for Marathon after a plague and an oracle declare that they had returned too early. They later make further attempts, eventually conquer the Peloponnese, and divide its cities by lot.

l: Peloponnese, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: A plague spreads throughout the Peloponnese after the Heraclids' premature return. The Heraclids eventually conquer the region and divide its principal territories.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Hyllus acts according to Hercules's commands by marrying Iole and seeking the return of the Heraclids.

l: oracle concerning the Heraclids' return, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The oracle first says that the Heraclids should await the third crop. It later explains that this means the third generation rather than three years, and that the narrows refer to the broad-bellied sea on the right of the Isthmus.

l: Hyllus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Hyllus marries Iole according to Hercules's commands and asks at Delphi how the Heraclids can return. He interprets the third crop as three years, returns with an army, and is defeated and killed.

l: Tisamenus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Tisamenus, son of Orestes, is reigning over the Peloponnesians when the Heraclids make an attempt to return. He is later killed by them after they defeat the enemy by land and sea.

l: Aristomachus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Aristomachus leads a later attempt to return after the earlier failures. He is defeated and killed in battle by the Peloponnesians.

l: Temenus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Temenus and his brothers consult the oracle about their return. He blames the god for their earlier misfortunes, then prepares the army, builds ships at Naupactus, and later receives Argos in the division of the conquered Peloponnese. His sons arrange his murder because he favors Hyrnetho and Deiphontes.

l: Cresphontes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Cresphontes uses a clod of earth instead of a stone in the drawing of lots so that he will receive Messene. He is later murdered with two of his sons after reigning there for a short time.

l: Aristodemus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Aristodemus is killed by a thunderbolt while the army is at Naupactus. He leaves twin sons, Eurysthenes and Procles, by Argia.

l: Naupactus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Naupactus is the place in Locris where Temenus builds ships for the expedition. The army suffers a calamity there when the soothsayer is killed, the ships are destroyed, and the land force is overcome by famine.

l: Aristodemus's army, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Aristodemus's army suffers disaster at Naupactus after Hippotes kills the soothsayer. Its ships are destroyed, its land force suffers famine, and the army disbands.

l: soothsayer Carnus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The soothsayer Carnus appears among the army, reciting oracles in a state of inspiration. The army mistakes him for a magician sent by the Peloponnesians, and Hippotes kills him with a javelin.

l: Hippotes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Hippotes kills the soothsayer with a javelin after mistaking him for an enemy agent. He is banished for ten years after the oracle attributes the army's calamity to the killing.

l: Three-eyed One, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The oracle commands the Heraclids to take the Three-eyed One as their guide. They interpret this instruction through Oxylus, who is found riding a one-eyed horse.

l: Oxylus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Oxylus, son of Andraemon, is found sitting on a one-eyed horse after returning from exile. The Heraclids interpret the oracle through him, make him their guide, and under his guidance defeat the enemy.

l: Peloponnesians, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The Peloponnesians defeat the Heraclids in an earlier battle and kill Aristomachus. They later lose to the Heraclids by land and sea under Oxylus's guidance.

l: conquest of Peloponnese, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The Heraclids conquer the Peloponnese after defeating the enemy by land and sea and killing Tisamenus. They then establish altars and divide the cities among their leaders.

l: drawing of lots for the cities, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: After conquering the Peloponnese, the leaders sacrifice at three altars and draw lots for the cities. Temenus and the sons of Aristodemus throw stones into a water-filled pitcher, while Cresphontes throws in a clod that dissolves.

l: Argos, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Argos is the first territory assigned in the drawing of lots. Its sign is a toad, which the seers interpret as advising its rulers to remain in the city.

l: Lacedaemon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Lacedaemon is the second territory assigned in the drawing of lots. Its sign is a serpent, interpreted by the seers as indicating rulers who would be terrible in attack.

l: Messene, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Messene is the third territory assigned. Cresphontes obtains it through his stratagem in the drawing of lots, and its sign is a fox, interpreted as indicating wily rulers.

l: Hyrnetho, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Hyrnetho is Temenus's daughter, and Temenus favors her and her husband Deiphontes over his sons. After Temenus's murder, the army assigns the kingdom to Hyrnetho and Deiphontes.

l: Deiphontes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Deiphontes is Hyrnetho's husband and is favored by Temenus. After Temenus is murdered, the army decides that the kingdom belongs to Deiphontes and Hyrnetho.

l: Cresphontes's wife Merope, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Merope is the wife of the murdered Cresphontes. Polyphontes takes her as his wife against her will, but she saves her third son Aepytus by sending him to her own father to be raised.

l: Polyphontes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Polyphontes, one of the true Heraclids, takes Merope as his wife after Cresphontes's murder and becomes king. Aepytus later secretly returns and kills him.

l: Aepytus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Aepytus is Merope's third son and is raised by his maternal grandfather. When he reaches manhood, he secretly returns, kills Polyphontes, and recovers his ancestral kingdom.

l: murder of Cresphontes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Cresphontes is murdered with two of his sons after he has ruled Messene for a short time. Polyphontes then takes Merope and the kingship.

l: murder of Polyphontes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: Polyphontes is secretly killed by Aepytus after Aepytus reaches manhood and returns. Aepytus then recovers the kingdom of his fathers.

l: return of the Heraclids, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. vir. 2
s: The Heraclids' first return causes a plague because it occurs before the proper time. After failed attempts and a corrected interpretation of the oracle, they return under Oxylus's guidance and conquer the Peloponnese.

l: The Library, The Library, BOOK III
s: The unit concludes the account of the family of Inachus from Belus to the Heraclids and begins the account of the house of Agenor. Libya and Poseidon had Belus and Agenor; Agenor went to Phoenicia, married Telephassa, and had Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix. Zeus carried Europa to Crete in the form of a tame bull, where she bore Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys. After Europa disappeared, Agenor sent his sons to search for her and ordered them not to return until they found her, while Telephassa accompanied them.

l: family of Inachus, The Library, BOOK III
s: The family of Inachus is described from Belus down to the Heraclids before the account turns to the house of Agenor.

l: Belus, The Library, BOOK III
s: Belus was a son of Libya and Poseidon. He reigned over the Egyptians and fathered the previously mentioned sons.

l: Heraclids, The Library, BOOK III
s: The Heraclids mark the endpoint of the family of Inachus described in this unit.

l: house of Agenor, The Library, BOOK III
s: The unit begins the account of the house of Agenor after describing the family of Inachus.

l: Libya (person), The Library, BOOK III
s: Libya had two sons by Poseidon, Belus and Agenor.

l: Poseidon, The Library, BOOK III
s: Poseidon fathered Belus and Agenor with Libya.

l: Agenor, The Library, BOOK III
s: Agenor went to Phoenicia, married Telephassa, and fathered Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix. After Europa disappeared, he sent his sons to search for her and ordered them not to return before finding her.

l: Phoenicia, The Library, BOOK III
s: Agenor went to Phoenicia, where he married Telephassa and had Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix.

l: Telephassa, The Library, BOOK III
s: Telephassa married Agenor and was the mother of Europa, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix. She accompanied the search for Europa.

l: Europa, The Library, BOOK III
s: Europa was described as a daughter of Agenor and Telephassa, although some said she was a daughter of Phoenix. Zeus desired her, carried her to Crete in the form of a tame bull, and fathered Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys with her. After she disappeared, Agenor sent her brothers to search for her.

l: Cadmus, The Library, BOOK III
s: Cadmus was a son of Agenor and Telephassa. He was sent with his brothers to search for Europa.

l: Phoenix, The Library, BOOK III
s: Phoenix was a son of Agenor and Telephassa. He was sent with his brothers to search for Europa.

l: Cilix, The Library, BOOK III
s: Cilix was a son of Agenor and Telephassa. He was sent with his brothers to search for Europa.

l: Zeus, The Library, BOOK III
s: Zeus desired Europa, transformed himself into a tame bull, carried her across the sea to Crete, and fathered Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys with her.

l: bull (Zeus's transformed form), The Library, BOOK III
s: The bull was Zeus in transformed form. As a tame bull, it carried Europa across the sea to Crete.

l: Crete, The Library, BOOK III
s: Crete was the place to which Zeus, in the form of a tame bull, carried Europa. Zeus fathered Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys with her there.

l: Minos, The Library, BOOK III
s: Minos was born to Europa after Zeus came together with her in Crete.

l: Sarpedon, The Library, BOOK III
s: Sarpedon was born to Europa after Zeus came together with her in Crete. Homer instead said that Sarpedon was born to Zeus and Laodameia, the daughter of Bellerophon.

l: Rhadamanthys, The Library, BOOK III
s: Rhadamanthys was born to Europa after Zeus came together with her in Crete.

l: search for Europa, The Library, BOOK III
s: The search for Europa began after she disappeared. Agenor ordered his sons to search for her and not return until they found her, and Telephassa accompanied them.

l: sons of Agenor, The Library, BOOK III
s: The sons of Agenor, Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, were sent to search for Europa after her disappearance. Agenor ordered them not to return until they found her, and Telephassa went with them.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The unit recounts the descendants of Europa, including the careers of Minos, Sarpedon, Rhadamanthys, and their families. It describes Minos’s rise to power in Crete, the birth and confinement of the Minotaur, and the construction of the Labyrinth. It tells how Cadmus founded Thebes after killing a dragon and sowing its teeth, then married Harmonia. It also relates the death and resurrection of Glaucus and the death of Actaeon after he saw Artemis bathing.

l: Europa, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Europa was carried by Zeus, who had taken the form of a tame bull, across the sea to Crete. She bore Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys, and Asterius later married her and raised her children.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Zeus carried Europa to Crete in the form of a tame bull and fathered Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamanthys by her. He granted Sarpedon life for three generations, married Harmonia to Cadmus, loved Semele, and changed Dionysus into a kid to evade Hera.

l: Minos, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Minos became king of Crete after Poseidon sent up a bull in response to his prayer, though he sacrificed another bull instead. He married Pasiphae, fathered several children, confined the Minotaur in the Labyrinth, and recovered Glaucus after Polyidus restored him to life.

l: Sarpedon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Sarpedon quarrelled with Minos over their love for Miletus and fled after Minos gained the advantage in war. He allied himself with Cilix against the Lycians, received part of the country, and became king of Lycia; Zeus granted him life for three generations.

l: Rhadamanthys, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Rhadamanthys made laws for the islanders, then fled to Boeotia and married Alcmena. After his death he judged in Hades with Minos.

l: Poseidon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Poseidon sent Minos a fine bull from the sea after Minos promised to sacrifice it. When Minos sacrificed another bull instead, Poseidon made the bull savage and caused Pasiphae to desire it.

l: Cadmus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Cadmus sought Europa, founded Thebes after following a divinely indicated cow, killed the dragon guarding the spring of Ares, and sowed its teeth. He served Ares for an eternal year, then received the kingdom and married Harmonia.

l: Catreus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Catreus was a son of Minos and father of Aerope, Clymene, Apemosyne, and Althaemenes. An oracle said that one of his children would kill him, and Althaemenes later killed him unknowingly when Catreus came to Rhodes.

l: Glaucus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Glaucus fell into a jar of honey while chasing a mouse and died. A serpent revived another serpent with an herb, and Polyidus used the same herb to restore Glaucus to life.

l: Pasiphae, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Pasiphae, the wife of Minos, was made by Poseidon to desire the bull that Minos had refused to sacrifice. With Daedalus’s help she joined with the bull and gave birth to the Minotaur.

l: Althaemenes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Althaemenes left Crete with his sister Apemosyne because he feared becoming his father’s murderer. In Rhodes he later killed Catreus unknowingly, then disappeared into a chasm after learning what he had done.

l: Polyidus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Polyidus identified the color of Minos’s three-colored cow by comparing it to the fruit of the bramble and found the dead Glaucus. He restored Glaucus to life with an herb and was forced to teach him divination.

l: Harmonia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Harmonia was the daughter of Aphrodite and Ares. Zeus gave her in marriage to Cadmus, and Cadmus gave her a robe and a necklace made by Hephaestus, according to one account.

l: Ares, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Ares was said to be the father of the dragon that guarded the spring near Thebes. Cadmus served Ares for an eternal year as atonement for killing the dragon.

l: Ino, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Ino was a daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia and married Athamas. She later became known as Leucothoe after plunging into the sea with her dead child.

l: Semele, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Semele was a daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia. Zeus loved her and secretly slept with her.

l: Actaeon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Actaeon, the son of Autonoe and Aristaeus, was trained as a hunter by Chiron. He was transformed into a deer and devoured by his own dogs after seeing Artemis bathing.

l: Artemis, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Artemis was seen bathing by Actaeon. She immediately transformed him into a deer and drove madness into his fifty dogs, which then devoured him.

l: Crete, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Crete was ruled by Minos, who passed laws there and extended his dominion over almost all the islands. It was also the destination of Europa and the place where Asterius raised her children.

l: Rhodes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Rhodes received Althaemenes and Apemosyne after they left Crete. Catreus later came to Rhodes intending to transfer his kingdom to Althaemenes, but Althaemenes killed him unknowingly there.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The Labyrinth was constructed by Daedalus and had tangled passages that confused the way out. Minos shut the Minotaur inside it and guarded him there.

l: Thebes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Thebes was founded by Cadmus at the place where the cow guiding him collapsed. Its foundation followed his killing of the dragon at the spring of Ares and his sowing of the dragon’s teeth.

l: Sparti, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The Sparti were armed men who sprang from the ground after Cadmus sowed the dragon’s teeth. They fought and killed one another, although five survived: Echion, Udaeus, Chthonius, Hyperenor, and Pelorus.

l: Minotaur, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The Minotaur was born to Pasiphae after she joined with Minos’s bull with Daedalus’s assistance. It had the face of a bull and the rest of its body human, and Minos confined it in the Labyrinth.

l: dragon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: A dragon guarded the spring of Ares and killed most of the men sent by Cadmus to fetch water. Cadmus killed it, and Athena advised him to sow its teeth.

l: Cretan Bull, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: A bull rose from the sea at Minos’s request to prove that he had received the kingdom from the gods. Minos spared that bull for his herds instead of sacrificing it, and Poseidon consequently made it savage and caused Pasiphae to desire it.

l: dragon’s teeth, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Athena advised Cadmus to sow the dragon’s teeth after he killed the dragon. Armed men called the Sparti grew from them and fought one another.

l: abduction of Europa, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The abduction of Europa occurred when Zeus, disguised as a tame bull, carried her over the sea to Crete. Her brothers and others searched for her but could not find her and settled in different places.

l: birth of the Minotaur, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The birth of the Minotaur followed Poseidon’s punishment of Minos for failing to sacrifice the bull. Daedalus built a wooden cow for Pasiphae, who joined with the bull and gave birth to Asterius, called the Minotaur.

l: foundation of Thebes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The foundation of Thebes began when Cadmus followed a cow in accordance with the oracle at Delphi. After the cow collapsed, Cadmus killed the dragon guarding the spring of Ares and established the city there.

l: sowing of the dragon’s teeth, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The sowing of the dragon’s teeth was performed by Cadmus on Athena’s advice. The teeth produced armed men, who became the Sparti and fought one another.

l: death and resurrection of Glaucus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Glaucus died after falling into a jar of honey while chasing a mouse. Polyidus saw a serpent revive another serpent with an herb, applied the herb to Glaucus, and restored him to life.

l: death of Actaeon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: Actaeon’s death followed his seeing Artemis bathing, according to the more common account. Artemis changed him into a deer and caused his dogs to become mad and devour him.

l: marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 111. 10
s: The marriage of Cadmus and Harmonia took place after Cadmus had completed his service to Ares. Zeus gave Harmonia to Cadmus, and the gods attended the wedding and celebrated it with hymns.

l: The Library, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Dionysus, after discovering the vine and being driven mad by Hera, wanders through Egypt and Syria before traveling through Phrygia, Thrace, India, and Greece. Lycurgus, king of the Edonians, expels Dionysus and is later driven mad and killed by the will of Dionysus. In Thebes, Dionysus causes the women to engage in Bacchic frenzy, and Pentheus is torn apart by his mother Agave on Cithaeron. Later, Tyrrhenian pirates attempt to take Dionysus past Naxos, but he turns their ship's mast and oars into snakes, causing the pirates to leap into the sea and become dolphins.

l: Dionysus, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Dionysus discovered the vine and, after Hera drove him mad, wandered through Egypt and Syria. He was received by Proteus in Egypt, purified by Rhea in Phrygia, and then traveled through Thrace, India, Thebes, and Argos. He drove Lycurgus and the women of Argos mad, defeated the Tyrrhenian pirates by transforming their ship, and brought his mother from Hades before ascending with her to heaven.

l: Egypt, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Egypt was one of the regions through which Dionysus wandered. Proteus, king of Egypt, received Dionysus.

l: Thrace, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Dionysus hastened through Thrace on his journey against the Indians. He later traversed Thrace and the whole of India before coming to Thebes.

l: Lycurgus, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Lycurgus, son of Dryas and king of the Edonians beside the Strymon, insulted and expelled Dionysus. Dionysus drove him mad, and after Lycurgus killed his son while mistaking him for a vine branch, Lycurgus was bound on Mount Pangaeum and killed by horses at Dionysus's will.

l: Bacchanals, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: The Bacchanals accompanying Dionysus were captured with the multitude of Satyrs when Lycurgus expelled him. They were later suddenly released, and Dionysus compelled the women to engage in Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron.

l: Thebes, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Dionysus came to Thebes after traveling through Thrace and India. There he forced the women to leave their homes and engage in Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron.

l: Cithaeron, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Cithaeron was the mountain where Dionysus compelled the women to engage in Bacchic frenzy. Pentheus came there to spy on the Bacchanals and was torn apart.

l: Pentheus, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Pentheus, born to Agave and Echion, had received the kingship after Cadmus and tried to prevent the Bacchic rites. He went to Cithaeron to spy on the Bacchanals, where his mother Agave, in a fit of madness, tore him limb from limb after mistaking him for a wild beast.

l: Agave, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Agave was the mother of Pentheus. In a fit of madness on Cithaeron, she mistook Pentheus for a wild beast and tore him limb from limb.

l: Naxos, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: Dionysus wished to be transported from Icaria to Naxos. The Tyrrhenian pirates carried him past Naxos while attempting to take him to Asia to sell him.

l: Tyrrhenian pirates, The Library, V. Διόνυσος δὲ εὑρετὴς ἀμπέλου γενόμενος,
s: The Tyrrhenian pirates hired out a trireme and carried Dionysus aboard, intending to sail to Asia and sell him instead of taking him to Naxos. Dionysus turned the mast and oars into snakes and filled the ship with ivy and the sound of flutes; the pirates went mad, leaped into the sea, and became dolphins.

l: The Library, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes and go to the Encheleans, who make them leaders against the Illyrians; Cadmus then reigns over the Illyrians, and later Zeus sends the pair to the Elysian Fields after transforming them into a serpent. Polydorus becomes king of Thebes, and after Labdacus dies, Lycus rules while Labdacus's son Laius is still a child. Zethus and Amphion, the sons of Antiope, kill Lycus and Dirce, fortify Thebes, and expel Laius. Laius later stays with Pelops and carries off Chrysippus while teaching him to drive a chariot.

l: Cadmus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Cadmus leaves Thebes with Harmonia and goes to the Encheleans. He leads the Encheleans against the Illyrians, defeats them, and reigns over the Illyrians. Illyrius is born to him, and later he is transformed into a serpent with Harmonia and sent to the Elysian Fields by Zeus.

l: Harmonia, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Harmonia leaves Thebes with Cadmus and goes to the Encheleans. She leads the Encheleans with Cadmus against the Illyrians, and later she is transformed into a serpent with Cadmus and sent to the Elysian Fields by Zeus.

l: Thebes, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Thebes is ruled by Polydorus and later by Lycus while Laius is a child. Zethus and Amphion take over, fortify the city, and expel Laius.

l: Encheleans, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: The Encheleans are attacked by the Illyrians. After receiving an oracle, they make Cadmus and Harmonia their leaders against the Illyrians and defeat them.

l: Illyrians, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: The Illyrians attack the Encheleans but are defeated when the Encheleans are led by Cadmus and Harmonia. Cadmus then reigns over them.

l: Polydorus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Polydorus becomes king of Thebes. He marries Nycteis, the daughter of Nycteus, and fathers Labdacus.

l: Nycteus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Nycteus is the son of Chthonius and the father of Nycteis and Antiope. He commands Lycus to punish Epopeus and Antiope, then kills himself in distress.

l: Labdacus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Labdacus is born to Polydorus and Nycteis. He dies after Pentheus because he shares a similar way of thinking, leaving his one-year-old son Laius.

l: Laius, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Laius is the one-year-old son left by Labdacus. Lycus rules while he is a child, and Zethus and Amphion later expel him from Thebes. In the Peloponnese, Laius is received by Pelops and carries off Chrysippus while teaching him to drive a chariot.

l: Lycus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Lycus, the brother of Nycteus, rules Thebes while Laius is a child and reigns for twenty years. He had fled with Nycteus after killing Phlegyas, later marched against Sicyon, killed Epopeus, and brought Antiope away captive. Zethus and Amphion kill him.

l: Zethus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Zethus is exposed with Amphion but is found and raised by a neatherd. He tends cattle, recognizes Antiope as his mother, kills Lycus with Amphion, kills Dirce, fortifies Thebes with Amphion, and expels Laius.

l: Amphion, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Amphion is exposed with Zethus but is found and raised by a neatherd. He practises minstrelsy with a lyre given to him by Hermes, recognizes Antiope as his mother, kills Lycus with Zethus, kills Dirce, and helps fortify Thebes, with the stones following his lyre.

l: Antiope, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Antiope is the daughter of Nycteus, and Zeus has intercourse with her. When she becomes pregnant, she flees to Epopeus at Sicyon and marries him; Nycteus later commands Lycus to punish her. She gives birth to Zethus and Amphion, is imprisoned and mistreated by Lycus and Dirce, and is later recognized and rescued by her sons.

l: Zeus, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Zeus has intercourse with Antiope. He later sends Cadmus and Harmonia to the Elysian Fields after they are transformed into a serpent.

l: Dirce, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Dirce is the wife of Lycus and mistreats the imprisoned Antiope. Zethus and Amphion bind her to a bull and throw her dead body into a spring that is thereafter called Dirce.

l: Illyrian war, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: The Illyrian war is fought when the Illyrians attack the Encheleans. The Encheleans, led by Cadmus and Harmonia, defeat the Illyrians.

l: Cadmus's and Harmonia's departure from Thebes, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes and go to the Encheleans. They become the leaders of the Encheleans against the Illyrians.

l: Cadmus's reign over the Illyrians, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: After leading the Encheleans to victory over the Illyrians, Cadmus reigns over the Illyrians. Illyrius is born to him during this reign.

l: fortification of Thebes, The Library, Ὁ δὲ Κάδμος pera ‘Appovias Θήβας ἐκλιπὼν
s: After killing Lycus and Dirce, Zethus and Amphion take over the sovereignty and fortify Thebes. The stones follow Amphion's lyre as the city is fortified.

l: The Library, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Zethus married Thebe, while Amphion married Niobe, who bore seven sons and seven daughters according to this account, though other traditions gave different numbers. Niobe claimed to be more blessed with children than Latona, provoking Artemis and Apollo to kill her children, after which Niobe became a stone at Sipylus. After Amphion’s death, Laius ruled Thebes, but Oedipus unknowingly killed Laius, solved the Sphinx’s riddle, became king, and married Jocasta. When the truth was revealed, Jocasta hanged herself, Oedipus blinded himself, was expelled from Thebes, and later died at Colonus.

l: Thebes, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Thebes was associated with Thebe, after whom the city was named. During Creon’s rule, the city suffered from the Sphinx until Oedipus solved her riddle; Oedipus then became its king.

l: Amphion, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Amphion married Niobe and was the only male said to have survived Apollo’s attack in one account. After Amphion’s death, Laius took over the kingdom; another account says that Amphion was also killed by Artemis and Apollo.

l: Niobe, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, married Amphion and bore seven sons and seven daughters in this account, though other writers gave different numbers. After claiming to be more blessed with children than Latona, she provoked Artemis and Apollo, and later became a stone at Sipylus whose tears flowed day and night.

l: Artemis, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Artemis was provoked against Niobe’s children after Niobe claimed to be more blessed with children than Latona. She shot the female children in the house.

l: Apollo, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Apollo was provoked against Niobe’s children together with Artemis. He killed the male children while they were hunting on Mount Cithaeron; another account says that he also killed Amphion.

l: Laius, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Laius succeeded to the kingdom after Amphion’s death and married a daughter of Menoeceus. An oracle warned him not to beget a son because the son would kill him, but Oedipus later killed Laius in a narrow road in Phocis.

l: Jocasta, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Jocasta was identified by some as the daughter of Menoeceus whom Laius married. She unknowingly married her son Oedipus, and after the hidden truth was revealed, she hanged herself.

l: Oedipus, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Oedipus was exposed as an infant after Laius pierced his ankles, but he was found and raised by Periboea. Believing himself to be the son of his nominal parents, he left Corinth, killed Laius and Polyphontes, solved the Sphinx’s riddle, became king of Thebes, and unknowingly married Jocasta. When the truth was revealed, he blinded himself, was expelled from Thebes, and later died at Colonus.

l: Creon, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Creon, son of Menoeceus, succeeded to the kingdom after Laius’s burial. During his rule, he proclaimed that whoever solved the Sphinx’s riddle would receive the kingdom and Laius’s wife, and he lost his son Haemon to the Sphinx.

l: Hera, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Hera sent the Sphinx against Thebes, bringing a major calamity upon the city.

l: Sphinx, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: The Sphinx, whose mother was Echidna and whose father was Typhon, had the face of a woman, the breast, feet, and tail of a lion, and the wings of a bird. She sat on Mount Phicium, posed her riddle to the Thebans, devoured those who could not answer it, and threw herself from the citadel after Oedipus solved it.

l: riddle of the Sphinx, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: The riddle asked what has one voice and becomes four-footed, two-footed, and three-footed. Oedipus answered that it was a human being, who crawls on four limbs as an infant, walks on two feet as an adult, and uses a staff as a third support in old age.

l: Niobe's children, The Library, Γαμεῖ δὲ Ζῆθος μὲν Θήβην, ad ἧς ἡ πόλιες
s: Niobe’s children are listed in this account as seven sons, Sipylus, Eupinytus, Ismenus, Damasichthon, Agenor, Phaedimus, and Tantalus, and seven daughters, Ethodaia, Cleodoxa, Astyoche, Phthia, Pelopia, Astycratia, and Ogygia. Artemis killed the daughters and Apollo killed the sons, although Amphion, Chloris, or in another account Amyclas and Meliboea were said to have survived; other writers gave different numbers of children.

l: The Library, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Eteocles and Polynices agree that they will rule the kingdom of Thebes in alternate years, but Eteocles refuses to surrender the kingdom after his year, so Polynices goes to Argos. Adrastus reconciles Polynices and Tydeus, marries them to his daughters, and promises to restore them to their homelands; he then gathers the Seven Champions for the war against Thebes. Eriphyle accepts Polynices' necklace and persuades Amphiaraus to join the expedition, despite his foreknowledge that the champions will die. At Nemea, Hypsipyle leads the champions to water while leaving Opheltes behind, and a serpent kills the child; the champions kill the serpent, bury Opheltes, and establish the Nemean Games in his honor.

l: Eteocles, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Eteocles agrees with Polynices that they will rule the kingdom in alternate years. According to one account, Eteocles rules first and refuses to surrender the kingdom; later, Tydeus tells him to yield it to Polynices, but he does not comply.

l: Polynices, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Polynices agrees with Eteocles to alternate rule of the kingdom, but after Eteocles refuses to surrender it, Polynices is banished from Thebes and goes to Argos with the necklace and robe. He marries Argia, gives Eriphyle the necklace, and asks her to persuade Amphiaraus to join the war. He is one of the champions who travels to Nemea, wins the wrestling match, and is later sent to demand that Eteocles yield the kingdom.

l: kingdom of Thebes, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: The kingdom is to be ruled by Eteocles and Polynices in alternate years. Eteocles refuses to hand it over to Polynices after his period of rule.

l: Thebes, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Polynices is banished from Thebes after Eteocles refuses to surrender the kingdom. The Seven Champions later prepare to march against Thebes.

l: Argos, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Argos is ruled by Adrastus. Polynices comes there after being banished from Thebes, and Adrastus gathers the champions there for the war against Thebes.

l: Adrastus, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Adrastus, son of Talaus, rules Argos and separates Polynices and Tydeus when they fight at night. Recalling a prophecy about yoking his daughters to a boar and a lion, he marries Deipyle to Tydeus and Argia to Polynices, promising to restore both men to their homelands. He gathers the Seven Champions for the war against Thebes, wins the horse race at Nemea, and later leads the army.

l: Tydeus, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Tydeus, son of Oeneus, has fled Calydon and fights Polynices at Adrastus's palace before Adrastus separates them. He marries Deipyle, joins the champions, wins the boxing match at Nemea, and is sent to tell Eteocles to yield the kingdom to Polynices. When fifty men ambush him, he kills all of them except Maeon.

l: Amphiaraus, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Amphiaraus, son of Oicles, is a seer who foresees that all the expedition's participants except Adrastus will die. He initially opposes the war, but Eriphyle persuades him to join after accepting the necklace; he then orders his sons to kill their mother and march against Thebes when they are grown. At Nemea, he explains that Opheltes's death foretells the future and wins the leaping and quoit-throwing contests.

l: Eriphyle, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Eriphyle is the person whose decision determines whether Amphiaraus will join the war. Although Amphiaraus forbids her to accept gifts from Polynices, she accepts his necklace and persuades Amphiaraus to march with Adrastus.

l: the Seven Champions, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: The Seven Champions are assembled by Adrastus for the war against Thebes. They include Adrastus, Amphiaraus, Capaneus, Hippomedon, Polynices, Tydeus, and Parthenopaeus, although another account replaces Polynices and Tydeus with Eteoclus and Mecisteus. They travel to Nemea, bury Opheltes after the child is killed, and later send Tydeus to demand that Eteocles yield the kingdom.

l: Nemea, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Nemea is ruled by Lycurgus. The champions come there seeking water, and events there include the death and burial of Opheltes and the establishment of the Nemean Games.

l: Hypsipyle, The Library, VI. ᾿Ἑτεοκλῆς δὲ καὶ ἸΠολυνείκης περὶ τῆς
s: Hypsipyle, who serves in Lycurgus's household, leads the champions to a spring while leaving behind the infant Opheltes whom she nurses. During her absence, a serpent kills Opheltes.
